newsitem.title: USA: Netanayhu visits King Hussein at start of U.S. trip.
newsitem.headline: Netanayhu visits King Hussein at start of U.S. trip.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met with Jordan's King Hussein at a Minnesota hospital on Sunday, calling him a "great friend of peace" but offering no clue as to whether the session helped unlock the stalled Middle East peace process.
"I was impressed that he was recovering so rapidly," Netanyahu said of the monarch who underwent routine prostate surgery on Saturday at the Mayo Clinic. "He is a great friend of peace."

The meeting lasted for about 45 minutes, after which Netanyahu headed for Washington where he has a crucial meeting on Monday with President Bill Clinton amid U.S. efforts to push the region toward peaceful resolution of the decades-long conflict.

The Israeli leader told a briefing he planned to talk to Clinton about efforts to "bring stability, end violence and bring the peace process forward. This is a wish many share ... we should do our utmost to achieve it."
Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali told reporters the visit was a "generous gesture" and "I hope this contact always bodes good for everybody around the world."

Arthur Avnon, Midwest consul-general for Israel, said the two leaders met alone in Hussein's hospital suite, speaking in English. He called the meeting a "gesture" that Netanyahu felt obligated to do, "a gesture of friendship and goodwill."
He said its importance was "probably that it took place" rather than whatever might have come from it.
Snow, blizzard-level winds and sub-freezing temperatures greeted the Israeli leader and his party in this medical centre city.

The 61-year-old Hussein was reported resting comfortably at Mayo's Methodist Hospital following routine surgery on Saturday in which a benign enlargement of his prostate was removed. Doctors said they found no sign of cancer that was removed during surgery at the same facility in 1962.
He will likely be released from the hospital this week.

The "Mayo Clinic mini-summit," as local press dubbed the meeting at the renowned medical facility where Hussein was recovering, had been seen as a chance for the Israeli leader to win more backing for proposed quick-pace negotiations to reach a comprehensive settlement over six months.

Jordan believes Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat would be wise to take Netanyahu up on his offer of rapid go-for-broke talks -- provided the Palestinians can get a clear picture from Israel on what the talks would encompass.
But Netanyahu showed no signs of backing away from the latest flashpoint in the crisis -- a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem that unleashed Palestinian rage.
"The construction in Jerusalem, the construction on Har Homa, will continue," the prime minister's cabinet secretary Danny Naveh told Israel army radio before the party flew to the United States.
Clashes have erupted nearly every day since Israel broke ground last month on Har Homa, a 6,500-home project on a hilltop that Palestinians call Jabal Abu Ghneim and on land each side claims.

Arafat was enroute to India to urge Non-Aligned Movement nations "to support Palestinian political rights and condemn the Israeli settlement activity," his adviser, Nabil Abu Rdainah, told Reuters on Sunday.
Palestinian cabinet minister Hanan Ashrawi was due in Washington to present Arafat's views to U.S. officials on the settlements and the future of Jerusalem.

The Palestinians have said Arafat will not negotiate with Netanyahu unless work stops on the new settlement. Israel, meanwhile, has accused Arafat of giving a green light to suicide bombings and said a crackdown against "terrorism" is a condition for future talks.
The Palestinian Centre for Public Opinion said on Sunday that 48.6 percent of 470 Palestinians polled backed suicide attacks against Israel as support sinks for peace talks.

U.S. officials said they had ideas for breaking the deadlock that would be put to Netanyahu and, by telephone, to Arafat. "We are developing our own ideas and we're going to put them forward," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
